promptHTML: In how many ways can 3600 be written as a product of two distinct positive integers a × b (where a ≠ b and the order does not matter, so a × b is the same as b × a)?
explanation: Factorise: 3600 = 2<sup>4</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>, so the number of divisors is (4+1)(2+1)(2+1) = 45. Since 45 is odd, 3600 is a perfect square (3600 = 60<sup>2</sup>), so one divisor pair is (60, 60) with a = b. Each unordered factorisation pairs a divisor with its complement; the 45 divisors form (45−1)/2 = 22 pairs of distinct factors plus the single repeated pair 60×60 (which is excluded because a ≠ b). Hence there are 22 valid ways. (23 wrongly includes the 60×60 pair.) The answer is D.

promptHTML: What is the exponent of 7 in the prime factorisation of 300! (the product of all integers from 1 to 300)? Equivalently, what is the largest integer k such that 7<sup>k</sup> divides 300! exactly?
explanation: By Legendre's formula, the exponent of a prime p in n! is ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p<sup>2</sup>⌋ + ⌊n/p<sup>3</sup>⌋ + …. Here ⌊300/7⌋ = 42, ⌊300/49⌋ = 6, ⌊300/343⌋ = 0. Sum = 42 + 6 = 48. (Stopping at the first term gives the trap 42; it forgets the extra multiples of 49.) The answer is E.

promptHTML: What is the sum of all the EVEN positive divisors of 1800?
explanation: Factorise: 1800 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>. The sum of ALL divisors is σ(1800) = (1+2+4+8)(1+3+9)(1+5+25) = 15 × 13 × 31 = 6045. The ODD divisors are exactly the divisors of the odd part 3<sup>2</sup>×5<sup>2</sup> = 225, whose divisor sum is (1+3+9)(1+5+25) = 13 × 31 = 403. The even divisors are all the rest, so their sum is 6045 − 403 = 5642. The answer is B.

promptHTML: What is the smallest positive integer by which 1512 must be multiplied so that the product becomes a perfect cube?
explanation: Factorise: 1512 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>3</sup> × 7. For a perfect cube every prime exponent must be a multiple of 3. The exponents of 2 and 3 are already 3 (fine); the exponent of 7 is 1, so it must be raised to 3, requiring two more factors of 7, i.e. multiply by 7<sup>2</sup> = 49. Check: 1512 × 49 = 74088 = 42<sup>3</sup>. (Multiplying by 7 gives 7<sup>2</sup>, still not a cube; 343 = 7<sup>3</sup> overshoots.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: A number is written as 2431 in base 5 (that is, the base-5 numeral whose digits are 2, 4, 3, 1). What is this same number expressed in base 8?
explanation: First convert 2431<sub>5</sub> to base 10: 2×5<sup>3</sup> + 4×5<sup>2</sup> + 3×5 + 1 = 2×125 + 4×25 + 15 + 1 = 250 + 100 + 15 + 1 = 366. Now convert 366 to base 8: 366 = 5×64 + 46, and 46 = 5×8 + 6, so the digits are 5, 5, 6, giving 556<sub>8</sub>. Check: 5×64 + 5×8 + 6 = 320 + 40 + 6 = 366. (366 is the base-10 value, the common trap of not converting.) The answer is A.

promptHTML: Three bells toll at intervals of 24, 36 and 54 seconds respectively. They all toll together exactly at 8:00:00 AM. How many more times will all three bells toll together during the next one hour (that is, after 8:00:00 AM up to and including 9:00:00 AM)?
explanation: All three toll together at multiples of LCM(24, 36, 54). Factorise: 24 = 2<sup>3</sup>×3, 36 = 2<sup>2</sup>×3<sup>2</sup>, 54 = 2×3<sup>3</sup>, so LCM = 2<sup>3</sup>×3<sup>3</sup> = 8×27 = 216 seconds. One hour = 3600 seconds, and ⌊3600/216⌋ = 16 (since 216×16 = 3456 ≤ 3600 < 3672 = 216×17). So after the 8:00:00 start there are 16 further simultaneous tolls (the 16th at 8:57:36; the 17th would come at 3672 s = 61 min 12 s past 8:00, i.e. 9:01:12, beyond the hour). The answer is B.

promptHTML: What is the largest positive integer that divides each of 1305, 4665 and 6905, leaving the SAME remainder in every case?
explanation: If a divisor d leaves the same remainder for all three numbers, then d divides each pairwise difference. Differences: 4665 − 1305 = 3360, 6905 − 4665 = 2240, 6905 − 1305 = 5600. The largest such d is gcd(3360, 2240, 5600). Now 3360 = 2<sup>5</sup>×3×5×7, 2240 = 2<sup>6</sup>×5×7, 5600 = 2<sup>5</sup>×5<sup>2</sup>×7; the common part is 2<sup>5</sup>×5×7 = 1120. Check: 1305 = 1120 + 185, 4665 = 4×1120 + 185, 6905 = 6×1120 + 185 — each leaves remainder 185. (185 is the common remainder, not the divisor.) The answer is A.

promptHTML: How many ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers satisfy LCM(x, y) = 7200? (Here (a, b) and (b, a) are counted as different ordered pairs.)
explanation: Factorise: 7200 = 2<sup>5</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>. Write x = 2<sup>a1</sup>3<sup>b1</sup>5<sup>c1</sup> and y = 2<sup>a2</sup>3<sup>b2</sup>5<sup>c2</sup>. The LCM condition means, for each prime, the larger of the two exponents equals the exponent in 7200. For a prime with exponent e, the number of ordered pairs (i, j) with max(i, j) = e is 2e + 1 (either i = e with j from 0..e, or j = e with i from 0..e−1). So the count is (2×5+1)(2×2+1)(2×2+1) = 11 × 5 × 5 = 275. (138 is the count of UNordered pairs; 54 is the total number of divisors.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: All 6 letters of the word MASTER (all distinct) are used to form every possible 6-letter "word," and these words are then listed in dictionary (alphabetical) order. What is the rank (position) of the word MASTER in this list?
explanation:
The letters in alphabetical order are A, E, M, R, S, T. Count how many words come strictly before MASTER, position by position.
1st letter M: letters before M are {A, E} = 2 letters. Each fixes the first letter and permutes the remaining 5: 2 × 5! = 2 × 120 = 240.
2nd letter A (smallest remaining {A,E,R,S,T}): 0 letters before it: 0 × 4! = 0.
3rd letter S, remaining pool {E,R,S,T}: before S are {E,R} = 2: 2 × 3! = 12.
4th letter T, remaining pool {E,R,T}: before T are {E,R} = 2: 2 × 2! = 4.
5th letter E, remaining pool {E,R}: before E = 0: 0 × 1! = 0.
6th letter R, remaining {R}: 0.
Words before MASTER = 240 + 0 + 12 + 4 + 0 + 0 = 256. So MASTER is at rank 256 + 1 = 257. (Choice 256 forgets the +1; 720 is the total count.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: Five men and five women are to be seated around a circular table (seats are distinguished only by who sits next to whom) so that the seats strictly alternate between men and women. In how many distinct ways can this be done?
explanation: Seat the men first. Around a circular table, arranging the 5 men in alternating positions fixes a circular pattern; the number of distinct circular arrangements of the 5 men is (5 − 1)! = 4! = 24. Once the men are seated, the 5 gaps between them are now distinguishable (each gap sits between two specific men), so the 5 women can be placed in those 5 gaps in 5! = 120 ways. Total = 24 × 120 = 2880. (Choice 14400 = 5! × 5! double-counts by not removing one rotational degree of freedom; 576 = 4! × 4! wrongly fixes both groups circularly.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: From 4 married couples (8 people in total), a committee of 4 people is to be selected. The committee must NOT contain both members of any single couple. How many such committees are possible?
explanation:
Since no couple may be fully represented, each chosen person must come from a different couple. A 4-person committee with no two people from the same couple must therefore draw exactly one person from each of the 4 couples. From each couple choose 1 of its 2 members: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 24 = 16.
Check by inclusion-exclusion: total C(8,4) = 70; subtract committees containing at least one full couple. Containing a chosen couple: 4 ways to pick that couple × C(6,2) = 15 for the other two seats = 60; add back those containing two full couples: C(4,2) = 6. Bad = 60 − 6 = 54, so good = 70 − 54 = 16. (70 is the unrestricted total; 54 is the count to subtract.) The answer is D.

promptHTML: In how many distinct arrangements of all 11 letters of the word MISSISSIPPI do no two S's stand next to each other? (The word contains one M, four I's, four S's, and two P's.)
explanation: First arrange the 7 non-S letters: M, I, I, I, I, P, P. The number of distinct arrangements of these is 7! / (4! × 2!) = 5040 / (24 × 2) = 105. Lining up 7 letters creates 8 gaps (including the two ends) into which S's may go: _ X _ X _ X _ X _ X _ X _ X _. To keep the four S's mutually non-adjacent, choose 4 of these 8 gaps, one S per chosen gap: C(8,4) = 70. Since all four S's are identical, no further factor is needed. Total = 105 × 70 = 7350. (34650 is the total number of arrangements with no restriction.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: A token starts at the origin (0,0) and moves to (5,5) on a grid, taking unit steps either one unit East (E) or one unit North (N). How many such monotonic paths never rise above the diagonal line y = x — that is, at every point (x, y) reached along the path, y ≤ x? (The path may touch the diagonal.)
explanation: A path from (0,0) to (5,5) uses 5 E's and 5 N's. The condition y ≤ x at every step means that reading the path left to right, the number of N's never exceeds the number of E's at any prefix — exactly the ballot/Dyck-path condition. The number of such paths is the 5th Catalan number: C<sub>5</sub> = C(10,5) / (5 + 1) = 252 / 6 = 42. (252 = C(10,5) is the count of all monotonic paths; 126 = 252/2 is the naive "half" answer that wrongly assumes symmetry handles the touching/boundary cases; 132 = C<sub>6</sub>.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: How many solutions in non-negative integers (x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>, x<sub>3</sub>, x<sub>4</sub>, x<sub>5</sub>) does the equation x<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub> + x<sub>3</sub> + x<sub>4</sub> + x<sub>5</sub> = 12 have, subject to x<sub>1</sub> ≥ 2 and x<sub>5</sub> ≥ 3 (the other three variables are unrestricted non-negative integers)?
explanation: Remove the lower bounds by substitution. Let y<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>1</sub> − 2 ≥ 0 and y<sub>5</sub> = x<sub>5</sub> − 3 ≥ 0, keeping x<sub>2</sub>, x<sub>3</sub>, x<sub>4</sub> as they are. The equation becomes y<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub> + x<sub>3</sub> + x<sub>4</sub> + y<sub>5</sub> = 12 − 2 − 3 = 7, with all five new variables ≥ 0. The number of non-negative integer solutions of a 5-variable sum equal to 7 is, by stars and bars, C(7 + 5 − 1, 5 − 1) = C(11, 4) = 330. (1820 = C(16,4) ignores both constraints; 495 = C(12,4) subtracts only one unit somewhere; 210 = C(10,4) over-subtracts.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: Using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 with no digit repeated, how many 4-digit numbers can be formed that are both even AND greater than 5000?
explanation:
A 4-digit number from these digits is greater than 5000 exactly when its thousands digit is in {5, 6, 7} (the smallest such, 5123, already exceeds 5000). It is even when its units digit is in {2, 4, 6}. The digit 6 lies in both sets, so split on whether 6 is used as the thousands or units digit.
Case A — units digit = 6: thousands digit from {5, 7} (2 choices); the two middle digits are any distinct choices from the remaining 5 digits in order: 5 × 4 = 20. Subtotal = 2 × 20 = 40.
Case B — units digit ∈ {2, 4} (2 choices) and units ≠ 6: thousands digit from {5, 6, 7} (3 choices); middle two from remaining 5: 5 × 4 = 20. Subtotal = 2 × 3 × 20 = 120.
Total = 40 + 120 = 160. (180 = 3 × 3 × 20 ignores the conflict over the shared digit 6.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: In how many ways can 12 distinct students be divided into 3 groups of 4 students each, when the groups are unlabeled (interchangeable — only who is grouped with whom matters)?
explanation: If the groups were labeled (Group A, B, C), the count would be the multinomial 12! / (4! × 4! × 4!) = C(12,4) × C(8,4) × C(4,4) = 495 × 70 × 1 = 34650. But the three groups are unlabeled and all have the same size 4, so each distinct partition has been counted 3! = 6 times (once for each way of labeling the three equal-size groups). Divide: 34650 / 6 = 5775. (34650 is the labeled count; 17325 = 34650/2 wrongly divides by 2! instead of 3!.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: On a city grid, a delivery rider travels from intersection (0,0) to intersection (6,5), at each step moving either one block East or one block North. To make two scheduled stops, the route must pass through BOTH the intersection (3,2) and the intersection (4,4). How many distinct routes satisfy this requirement?
explanation:
Any valid East/North route reaches the two checkpoints in the order (3,2) then (4,4), since both coordinates increase. Split the journey into three legs and multiply the path counts.
Leg 1 — (0,0) to (3,2): 3 E and 2 N steps, C(5,2) = 10 ways.
Leg 2 — (3,2) to (4,4): 1 E and 2 N steps, C(3,1) = 3 ways.
Leg 3 — (4,4) to (6,5): 2 E and 1 N steps, C(3,1) = 3 ways.
Total = 10 × 3 × 3 = 90. (462 = C(11,5) counts all routes ignoring the stops; 200 counts routes through (3,2) only; 210 counts routes through (4,4) only.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: Anu and Bob each agree to arrive at a cafe at some moment chosen independently and uniformly at random between 5:00 pm and 6:00 pm. Whoever arrives first waits exactly 20 minutes for the other and then leaves. What is the probability that the two actually meet?
explanation: Let x and y be the arrival times in minutes after 5:00, each uniform on [0, 60], so (x, y) is uniform over a 60×60 square of area 3600. They meet exactly when |x − y| ≤ 20. It is easier to find the complement: |x − y| > 20 consists of two right triangles, each with legs of length 60 − 20 = 40. Each triangle has area ½×40×40 = 800, so the 'miss' region has area 1600. Thus P(miss) = 1600/3600 = 4/9, and P(meet) = 1 − 4/9 = 5/9. (Choosing 4/9 forgets to take the complement; 1/3 wrongly uses 20/60.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: An urn contains 3 red balls and 2 black balls. The balls are drawn one at a time, without replacement, until the urn is empty. What is the probability that the second red ball drawn appears exactly on the 4th draw?
explanation: Treat all 5 balls as occupying 5 ordered positions, with the 3 red positions equally likely to be any 3 of the 5 slots: there are C(5,3) = 10 equally likely arrangements of the reds. We need the 2nd red to land exactly in position 4, which requires exactly one red among the first three positions and a red in position 4 (the third red then occupies position 5). So the red positions are {one of positions 1-3, position 4, position 5}; there are 3 choices for the single early red, giving 3 favorable arrangements. The probability is 3/10. (2/5 is the maximum, attained at position 3, a tempting wrong pick.) The answer is A.

promptHTML: A drawer holds 5 identical-looking keys, exactly one of which opens a certain lock. You try the keys one at a time, without replacement, until the lock opens. Given that the first two keys you tried did NOT open the lock, what is the probability that the third key you try opens it?
explanation: By symmetry, before any information each key is equally likely to be the correct one, so the lock opens on try k with probability 1/5 for each k from 1 to 5. We are told the correct key is not among the first two tried, which had prior probability 3/5. Then P(opens on 3rd | not in first two) = P(opens on 3rd)/P(not in first two) = (1/5)/(3/5) = 1/3. Equivalently, given the failures, the correct key is equally likely to be any of the 3 untried keys, so the next try succeeds with probability 1/3. (Answer 1/5 ignores the conditioning.) The answer is D.

promptHTML: Two boxes sit on a table. Box 1 contains 2 gold coins and 3 silver coins; Box 2 contains 4 gold coins and 1 silver coin. A box is selected at random, but not equally: Box 2 is twice as likely to be chosen as Box 1. One coin is then drawn at random from the chosen box and it turns out to be gold. What is the probability that the coin came from Box 2?
explanation: The prior probabilities are P(Box 1) = 1/3 and P(Box 2) = 2/3. The chance of drawing gold from each box is P(gold | Box 1) = 2/5 and P(gold | Box 2) = 4/5. By total probability, P(gold) = (1/3)(2/5) + (2/3)(4/5) = 2/15 + 8/15 = 10/15 = 2/3. By Bayes' rule, P(Box 2 | gold) = [(2/3)(4/5)] / (2/3) = (8/15)/(10/15) = 8/10 = 4/5. (Choosing 2/3 just reuses the prior and ignores the gold evidence; 1/5 is P(Box 1 | gold).) The answer is E.

promptHTML: You roll a fair six-sided die repeatedly and stop the moment a 6 first appears. For every roll that shows a number other than 6 you earn $2, but on the final roll (the one that shows the 6) you pay a $5 penalty. What is the expected value of your net earnings for the whole game?
explanation: The number of rolls until the first 6 is geometric with success probability 1/6, so its expectation is 6. Of these, the last roll is the 6, so the expected number of non-6 rolls (each worth $2) is 6 − 1 = 5. Hence the expected gain from non-6 rolls is 2 × 5 = $10, and you always pay the $5 penalty on the terminal six. Net expected value = 10 − 5 = $5. (Using 6 instead of 5 non-six rolls gives the trap value 2×6 − 5 = $7.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: A committee of 4 people is to be chosen at random from a group of 7 men and 3 women. What is the probability that the committee contains at least 2 women?
explanation: The total number of committees is C(10,4) = 210. 'At least 2 women' means exactly 2 or exactly 3 women (there are only 3 women). Exactly 2 women: C(3,2)×C(7,2) = 3×21 = 63. Exactly 3 women: C(3,3)×C(7,1) = 1×7 = 7. So favorable = 63 + 7 = 70, and the probability is 70/210 = 1/3. (Equivalently, subtract P(0 women)=35/210 and P(1 woman)=105/210 from 1.) The trap 5/6 answers 'at least 1 woman', and 3/10 is 'exactly 2 women'. The answer is C.

promptHTML: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Given that the sum of the two numbers shown is even, what is the probability that the product of the two numbers is divisible by 4?
explanation: The sum is even exactly when both dice are even or both are odd. Both even: 3×3 = 9 outcomes; both odd: 3×3 = 9 outcomes; so the conditioning event has 18 outcomes. For the product to be divisible by 4: if both numbers are odd, the product is odd, never divisible by 4 (0 of those 9). If both are even, each is a multiple of 2, so the product carries at least 2×2 = 4 and is always divisible by 4 (all 9 of those qualify). Favorable = 9 out of 18, giving 9/18 = 1/2. (5/12 is the unconditional probability that the product is divisible by 4, ignoring the given even-sum condition.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: A straight stick of length 1 is broken at two points whose positions are chosen independently and uniformly at random along its length, producing three pieces. What is the probability that the three resulting pieces can be arranged to form a triangle?
explanation: Let the two break points be x and y, chosen uniformly and independently on [0, 1]; the point (x, y) is uniform over the unit square. The three pieces can form a triangle exactly when every piece is shorter than 1/2 (if any piece were ≥ 1/2 it would exceed the sum of the other two, violating the triangle inequality). Splitting by which break is on the left, in the region x < y the three pieces are x, y − x, 1 − y, and the conditions x < 1/2, y > 1/2, y − x < 1/2 cut out a triangle of area 1/8; the symmetric region x > y contributes another 1/8. Total favorable area = 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4. So the probability is 1/4. (1/2 is a common wrong guess from mishandling the inequalities.) The answer is B.

promptHTML:
Every one of 220 gym members is enrolled in at least one of three classes: Yoga, Pilates, or Spin.

• 130 are enrolled in Yoga, 110 in Pilates, and 85 in Spin.
• Exactly 140 members are enrolled in exactly one of the three classes.

How many members are enrolled in all three classes?
explanation:
Let the numbers enrolled in exactly one, exactly two, and exactly three classes be a, b, c. Since everyone takes at least one class, a + b + c = 220. We are told a = 140, so b + c = 80.

Now sum the three class sizes. A member in exactly one class is counted once, in exactly two classes is counted twice, and in all three is counted three times:
130 + 110 + 85 = a + 2b + 3c, i.e. 325 = 140 + 2b + 3c, so 2b + 3c = 185.

Subtract twice the relation b + c = 80 (which gives 2b + 2c = 160) from 2b + 3c = 185:
c = 185 − 160 = 25.

(Then b = 55, and a + b + c = 140 + 55 + 25 = 220 checks out.) Note 55 is the exactly-two count, not the answer; and (325−220)/2 = 52.5 is the wrong 'two-set' shortcut. The answer is E.

promptHTML:
In a group of 200 students, 150 use the Library, 120 use the Lab, and 90 use the Gym during a given week. A student may use any number of these three facilities, including none.

What is the largest possible number of students who use none of the three facilities that week?
explanation:
The number using 'none' is maximized when the number using at least one facility is minimized. The set of users must contain everyone who uses the Library (150), so it has at least 150 students. We can make it exactly 150 by placing all Lab users (120 ≤ 150) and all Gym users (90 ≤ 150) inside that same group of 150 Library users — this is possible because each smaller set fits within the largest.

So the minimum possible number of users is max(150, 120, 90) = 150, giving a maximum 'none' count of 200 − 150 = 50.

Traps: 200 − (150+120+90) treats the totals as disjoint (impossible here); 200 − 90 = 110 wrongly uses the smallest set. The answer is A.

promptHTML:
Each of 300 tourists visited at least one of three cities: Athens, Berlin, or Cairo.

• 180 visited Athens, 150 visited Berlin, 120 visited Cairo.
• 80 visited both Athens and Berlin, 60 visited both Berlin and Cairo, 50 visited both Athens and Cairo.

How many tourists visited exactly two of the three cities?
explanation:
Let t be the number who visited all three cities. By inclusion-exclusion, since everyone visited at least one city the union is 300:
300 = (180+150+120) − (80+60+50) + t = 450 − 190 + t = 260 + t, so t = 40.

The pairwise-overlap counts include those who visited all three. The number who visited exactly two equals the sum of pairwise overlaps minus three times the triple overlap (each all-three tourist is counted in all three pairwise totals):
exactly two = 190 − 3(40) = 190 − 120 = 70.

(Check: exactly one = 450 − 2×190 + 3×40 = 190; 190 + 70 + 40 = 300.) The trap 190 forgets to remove the triple-counted all-three visitors. The answer is B.

promptHTML:
In a class of 50 students, every student plays chess, table tennis, both, or neither. The total number who play chess is exactly twice the total number who play table tennis. 12 students play both games, and 2 students play neither.

How many students play chess?
explanation:
Let x be the total number who play table tennis; then the total who play chess is 2x. The number who play at least one game is 50 − 2 (neither) = 48.

By inclusion-exclusion for two sets:
(chess) + (table tennis) − (both) = (at least one)
2x + x − 12 = 48, so 3x = 60 and x = 20.

Therefore chess = 2x = 40. (Check: table tennis = 20, both = 12, so chess-only = 28 and TT-only = 8; 28 + 8 + 12 = 48, valid.)

Traps: 20 is the table-tennis total, not chess; 48 is the number playing at least one game; 28 = 40 − 12 subtracts 'both' incorrectly. The answer is C.

promptHTML:
A club of 250 members was surveyed about three magazines: A, B, and C.

• 120 read A, 110 read B, 100 read C.
• Exactly 18 members read all three magazines.
• Exactly 70 members read at least two of the three magazines.

How many members read none of the three magazines?
explanation:
From 'at least two = 70' and 'all three = 18', the number reading exactly two is 70 − 18 = 52.

The sum of the three pairwise-overlap counts (|A∩B| + |B∩C| + |A∩C|) counts each exactly-two reader once and each all-three reader three times, so it equals 52 + 3(18) = 52 + 54 = 106.

By inclusion-exclusion, the number reading at least one magazine is:
(120+110+100) − 106 + 18 = 330 − 106 + 18 = 242.

Therefore none = 250 − 242 = 8.

Traps: using 70 directly as the pairwise-overlap sum, or forgetting to add back the all-three term, both push the union above 250 (giving an impossible negative 'none'). The answer is D.

promptHTML:
In a neighborhood of 400 people, 220 own a dog, 180 own a cat, and 90 own a bird. Exactly 50 people own none of these pets, and exactly 30 people own all three.

How many people own exactly one of the three pets?
explanation:
The number owning at least one pet is 400 − 50 = 350.

By inclusion-exclusion: 350 = (220+180+90) − (sum of pairwise overlaps) + 30. With the set-size total 490, this gives:
sum of pairwise overlaps = 490 + 30 − 350 = 170.

The number owning exactly two pets equals the pairwise-overlap sum minus three times the all-three count: 170 − 3(30) = 170 − 90 = 80.

The 350 owners split into exactly-one, exactly-two, and all-three groups:
exactly one = 350 − 80 − 30 = 240.

Traps: 320 = 350 − 30 forgets the exactly-two group; 80 is the exactly-two count itself. The answer is B.

promptHTML: A car leaves a depot travelling along a straight highway at a constant 40 km/h. Exactly 3 hours later a motorcycle leaves the same depot along the same highway at a constant 60 km/h, chasing the car. How far from the depot is the point at which the motorcycle draws level with the car?
explanation: When the motorcycle starts, the car is already 40 × 3 = 120 km ahead. The motorcycle closes this gap at the relative speed 60 − 40 = 20 km/h, so it needs 120 / 20 = 6 hours to catch up. In those 6 hours the motorcycle covers 60 × 6 = 360 km, which is the distance from the depot. (Check: the car's total time is 3 + 6 = 9 h, distance 40 × 9 = 360 km — equal, confirming the meeting point.) The answer is A.

promptHTML: An escalator moves steadily upward at a constant number of steps per second. A boy who climbs at 1 step per second reaches the top having counted 25 steps under his own feet. A girl who climbs at 2 steps per second reaches the top having counted 40 steps. How many steps are visible on the escalator when it is switched off?
explanation: Let the escalator contribute e steps per second and N be the visible steps. The boy at 1 step/s takes 25 s to make his 25 steps, during which the escalator adds 25e steps, so N = 25 + 25e. The girl at 2 steps/s takes 40/2 = 20 s, so N = 40 + 20e. Equating: 25 + 25e = 40 + 20e ⇒ 5e = 15 ⇒ e = 3. Then N = 25 + 25(3) = 100 (and N = 40 + 20(3) = 100 checks). The answer is D.

promptHTML: A vessel contains 64 litres of pure milk. The following operation is performed three times in succession: a fixed quantity of x litres is drawn off and replaced by x litres of water, the mixture being stirred uniformly each time. After the three operations the ratio of milk to water in the vessel is 27 : 37. Find x.
explanation: After three identical draw-and-replace operations the fraction of original milk remaining is (1 − x/64)³. Since milk : water = 27 : 37, milk is 27/(27+37) = 27/64 of the 64 litres. So (1 − x/64)³ = 27/64. Taking cube roots, and using 27/64 = (3/4)³, we get 1 − x/64 = 3/4. Thus x/64 = 1/4 and x = 16. (Check: (1 − 16/64)³ = (3/4)³ = 27/64.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: A trader mixes two varieties of rice, one costing ₹50 per kg and the other ₹75 per kg, in the ratio 3 : 2 by weight. He sells the whole mixture at a profit of 25%. At what price per kg does he sell the mixture?
explanation: Per 5 kg of mixture there are 3 kg at ₹50 (= ₹150) and 2 kg at ₹75 (= ₹150), a total cost of ₹300 for 5 kg, i.e. a cost price of ₹60 per kg. Selling at 25% profit gives 60 × 1.25 = ₹75 per kg. (The ₹78.75 trap uses the reversed 2 : 3 ratio, giving a cost of ₹63 per kg.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: A 180-metre-long train running at 54 km/h is on the same track as, and behind, a 120-metre-long train running in the same direction at 36 km/h. How long does the faster train take to completely overtake (pass) the slower one, measured from when its front reaches the slower train's rear until its rear clears the slower train's front?
explanation: Convert speeds: 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 36 km/h = 10 m/s. Since they move the same way, the relative speed is 15 − 10 = 5 m/s. To overtake completely, the faster train must cover the combined length 180 + 120 = 300 m relative to the slower train. Time = 300 / 5 = 60 seconds. (The 12 s trap uses the opposite-direction relative speed 25 m/s.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: Working alone, Arun can finish a task in 10 days and Bela can finish the same task in 15 days. They work on alternate days — Arun on day 1, Bela on day 2, Arun on day 3, and so on. In how many days is the task completed?
explanation: Arun's daily work is 1/10, Bela's is 1/15. Over each Arun–Bela pair of days they complete 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 of the task. After 5 such pairs (10 days) they have done 5/6, with 1/6 left. Day 11 is Arun's: he does 1/10, leaving 1/6 − 1/10 = 5/30 − 3/30 = 2/30 = 1/15. Day 12 is Bela's: she does exactly 1/15, finishing the job. Total = 12 days. (6 days is the trap from assuming they always work together.) The answer is E.

promptHTML: What are the last two digits of the power tower 23<sup>(23<sup>23</sup>)</sup> ?
explanation:
The last two digits means the value mod 100. Since gcd(23, 100) = 1, exponents can be reduced modulo the Carmichael function λ(100) = lcm(λ(4), λ(25)) = lcm(2, 20) = 20 (Euler's totient φ(100) = 40 also works here). So we need the exponent 2323 mod 20.

Compute 2323 mod 20: 23 ≡ 3 (mod 20). The powers of 3 mod 20 cycle with period 4: 31 = 3, 32 = 9, 33 = 27 ≡ 7, 34 = 81 ≡ 1. Since 23 ≡ 3 (mod 4), 323 ≡ 33 ≡ 7 (mod 20). So the exponent is ≡ 7 (mod 20).

Therefore 23(2323) ≡ 237 (mod 100). Reduce step by step: 232 = 529 ≡ 29; 234 ≡ 292 = 841 ≡ 41; 237 = 234 · 232 · 23 ≡ 41 × 29 × 23. Now 41 × 29 = 1189 ≡ 89, and 89 × 23 = 2047 ≡ 47 (mod 100). So the last two digits are 47.

(A common trap is to compute only the single level 2323 mod 100 = 67, ignoring the tower.) The answer is 47.

promptHTML: What is the smallest positive integer N that simultaneously leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5, remainder 3 when divided by 7, remainder 4 when divided by 9, and remainder 5 when divided by 11?
explanation:
The four moduli 5, 7, 9, 11 are pairwise coprime, so by the Chinese Remainder Theorem there is a unique solution modulo 5 × 7 × 9 × 11 = 3465. Solve in stages.

Start with N ≡ 2 (mod 5) and N ≡ 3 (mod 7). Write N = 5k + 2; then 5k + 2 ≡ 3 (mod 7), so 5k ≡ 1 (mod 7). Since 5−1 ≡ 3 (mod 7) (because 5 × 3 = 15 ≡ 1), k ≡ 3 (mod 7). Thus N ≡ 5(3) + 2 = 17 (mod 35).

Combine with N ≡ 4 (mod 9). Write N = 35m + 17; then 35m + 17 ≡ 4 (mod 9), i.e. 8m + 8 ≡ 4, so 8m ≡ −4 ≡ 5 (mod 9). Since 8 ≡ −1, this is −m ≡ 5, so m ≡ 4 (mod 9). Then N ≡ 35(4) + 17 = 157 (mod 315).

Combine with N ≡ 5 (mod 11). Write N = 315t + 157; then 315t + 157 ≡ 5 (mod 11). Now 315 = 28·11 + 7 so 315 ≡ 7, and 157 = 14·11 + 3 so 157 ≡ 3. Thus 7t + 3 ≡ 5, so 7t ≡ 2 (mod 11). Since 7−1 ≡ 8 (mod 11) (7 × 8 = 56 ≡ 1), t ≡ 16 ≡ 5 (mod 11). The smallest non-negative t is 5, giving N = 315(5) + 157 = 1575 + 157 = 1732.

Check: 1732 = 5·346 + 2, = 7·247 + 3, = 9·192 + 4, = 11·157 + 5. The answer is 1732.

promptHTML: From an external point P, a tangent line touches a circle at T with PT = 10. A secant line from P cuts the circle at A (the nearer point) and B (the farther point). It is given that PB = 4 × PA. What is the length of the chord AB?
explanation:
By the power of a point P, the square of the tangent length equals the product of the two secant segments measured from P: PT2 = PA · PB.

We are told PB = 4 · PA, so substitute: PT2 = PA · (4 · PA) = 4 · PA2. With PT = 10 this gives 100 = 4 · PA2, so PA2 = 25 and PA = 5.

Then PB = 4 × 5 = 20. Since A lies between P and B on the secant, the chord AB = PB − PA = 20 − 5 = 15.

Verify the power relation: PA · PB = 5 × 20 = 100 = 102 = PT2. (Common traps: stopping at PA = 5, reporting the far distance PB = 20, or copying PT = 10.) The answer is 15.

promptHTML: Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle, and its diagonal AC is a diameter of the circle. The sides satisfy AB = 7, BC = 24, and AD = 15. What is the length of the other diagonal, BD?
explanation:
Because AC is a diameter, every angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle, so ∠ABC = 90° and ∠ADC = 90°. Thus triangles ABC and ADC are right-angled at B and D respectively, with AC as common hypotenuse.

From right triangle ABC: AC = √(AB2 + BC2) = √(72 + 242) = √(49 + 576) = √625 = 25 (the 7−24−25 triple). So the diameter AC = 25.

From right triangle ADC: DC = √(AC2 − AD2) = √(625 − 225) = √400 = 20 (the 15−20−25 triple).

Now apply Ptolemy's theorem to cyclic quadrilateral ABCD: the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides:
AC · BD = AB · CD + BC · AD.
So 25 · BD = 7 × 20 + 24 × 15 = 140 + 360 = 500, giving BD = 500 ÷ 25 = 20.

(Traps: forgetting the diameter forces right angles, or reusing a side length such as 15 or 24.) The answer is 20.

promptHTML: In how many ways can 12 identical balls be distributed among 5 distinct boxes so that exactly two of the boxes end up empty?
explanation:
Split the task into two independent choices. First, choose which 2 of the 5 distinct boxes are the empty ones: this can be done in C(5, 2) = 10 ways.

Second, the remaining 3 boxes must together hold all 12 identical balls with each of these 3 boxes receiving at least 1 ball (otherwise more than two boxes would be empty). The number of positive-integer solutions of y1 + y2 + y3 = 12 with every yi ≥ 1 is, by stars and bars, C(12 − 1, 3 − 1) = C(11, 2) = 55.

Since the two choices are independent, multiply: 10 × 55 = 550.

(Traps: forgetting the 'at least 1' surjection requirement and using C(13, 2) = 78 per choice, giving 780; or omitting the box-selection factor and reporting just 55.) The answer is 550.

promptHTML: Eight distinct people are to be seated in a single row of 8 chairs. Among them there are three particular pairs of feuding people: (P<sub>1</sub>, P<sub>2</sub>), (P<sub>3</sub>, P<sub>4</sub>), and (P<sub>5</sub>, P<sub>6</sub>) — six distinct individuals forming three disjoint pairs. In how many arrangements is it true that no feuding pair sits in two adjacent chairs?
explanation:
Use inclusion-exclusion on the three 'bad' events, where event Ei is 'the i-th feuding pair sits together'. Total unrestricted arrangements of 8 distinct people: 8! = 40320.

For a chosen set of k pairs forced together, glue each such pair into a single block (the two people inside can be ordered in 2! ways), leaving 8 − k objects to arrange: (8 − k)! × 2k arrangements, and there are C(3, k) ways to choose which pairs are glued.

k = 1: C(3,1) · 21 · 7! = 3 × 2 × 5040 = 30240.
k = 2: C(3,2) · 22 · 6! = 3 × 4 × 720 = 8640.
k = 3: C(3,3) · 23 · 5! = 1 × 8 × 120 = 960.

By inclusion-exclusion, the number with no feuding pair adjacent is
8! − 30240 + 8640 − 960 = 40320 − 30240 + 8640 − 960 = 17760.

(Traps: stopping after one subtraction gives 40320 − 30240 = 10080; mis-signing the terms or dropping the 2k block factor gives 25200 or 30240.) The answer is 17760.

promptHTML: A real number x satisfies √(x + 15) + √x = 15. What is the value of x?
explanation: Multiply both sides by the conjugate: (√(x+15) − √x)(√(x+15) + √x) = (x+15) − x = 15. Since the sum equals 15, the difference must equal 15/15 = 1, so √(x+15) − √x = 1. Adding this to the original equation: 2√(x+15) = 16, so √(x+15) = 8 and x + 15 = 64, giving x = 49. Check: √64 + √49 = 8 + 7 = 15. (Choosing 64 is the classic slip of solving for x + 15 instead of x.) The answer is D.

promptHTML: Positive integers x and y satisfy xy + x + y = 23 and x<sup>2</sup>y + xy<sup>2</sup> = 120. What is the value of x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup>?
explanation: Let s = x + y and p = xy. The first equation gives p + s = 23. The second is xy(x + y) = ps = 120. So s and p are roots of t² − 23t + 120 = 0, i.e. (t − 8)(t − 15) = 0, giving {s, p} = {8, 15}. If s = 15, p = 8, then x and y solve t² − 15t + 8 = 0, which has no integer roots. So s = 8, p = 15, giving integers x = 3, y = 5. Then x² + y² = s² − 2p = 64 − 30 = 34. (209 comes from wrongly taking s = 15, p = 8.) The answer is A.

promptHTML: A train covers a fixed route at a constant speed. If its speed were 10 km/h greater, it would take 1 hour less; if its speed were 10 km/h smaller, it would take 1.5 hours more. What is the length of the route, in km?
explanation: Let the speed be v and distance D. Faster case: D/v − D/(v+10) = 1, so 10D = v(v+10). Slower case: D/(v−10) − D/v = 1.5, so 10D = 1.5·v(v−10). Setting them equal: v + 10 = 1.5(v − 10), so v + 10 = 1.5v − 15, giving 0.5v = 25 and v = 50 km/h. Then 10D = 50 × 60 = 3000, so D = 300 km. Check: at 50 km/h the trip takes 6 h; at 60 km/h it takes 5 h (1 less); at 40 km/h it takes 7.5 h (1.5 more). The answer is C.

promptHTML: The quadratic equation x<sup>2</sup> + bx + 72 = 0 has two integer roots (not necessarily distinct). How many different integer values of b are possible?
explanation: If the integer roots are p and q, then pq = 72 and b = −(p + q). Since 72 > 0, the roots have the same sign. Positive factor pairs of 72: (1,72), (2,36), (3,24), (4,18), (6,12), (8,9), giving sums 73, 38, 27, 22, 18, 17 — six distinct values, hence six negative values of b. The negative pairs give the same six sums with opposite sign, hence six positive values of b. No pair has equal roots (72 is not a perfect square), and no overlap occurs, so there are 6 + 6 = 12 values. (Answering 6 forgets the negative-root pairs; 24 double-counts ordered pairs.) The answer is E.

promptHTML: Let x be the positive root of x<sup>2</sup> − x − 1 = 0. Then x<sup>5</sup> can be written as ax + b, where a and b are integers. What is a + b?
explanation: From x² = x + 1, reduce powers step by step. x³ = x·x² = x² + x = (x + 1) + x = 2x + 1. x⁴ = x·x³ = 2x² + x = 2(x + 1) + x = 3x + 2. x⁵ = x·x⁴ = 3x² + 2x = 3(x + 1) + 2x = 5x + 3. So a = 5, b = 3 and a + b = 8. (The coefficients are Fibonacci numbers; picking 7 or 13 comes from stopping one power too early or going one too far.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: Two candles of equal length are lit at the same moment. The first burns down completely in 4 hours and the second in 3 hours, each at its own constant rate. After how much time will the first candle be exactly twice as long as the second?
explanation: Take each candle's initial length as 1. After t hours the first has length 1 − t/4 and the second 1 − t/3. Require 1 − t/4 = 2(1 − t/3), i.e. 1 − t/4 = 2 − 2t/3. Then 2t/3 − t/4 = 1, so (8t − 3t)/12 = 1, giving 5t/12 = 1 and t = 12/5 hours = 2.4 hours = 2 hours 24 minutes. Check: at t = 2.4, lengths are 1 − 0.6 = 0.4 and 1 − 0.8 = 0.2, and 0.4 = 2 × 0.2. The answer is C.

promptHTML:
For x > 1, what is the minimum value of

4x + 9/(x − 1) ?
explanation: Rewrite so the two variable parts have constant product: 4x + 9/(x − 1) = 4(x − 1) + 9/(x − 1) + 4. For x > 1 both terms are positive, so by AM–GM, 4(x − 1) + 9/(x − 1) ≥ 2√(4 × 9) = 12, with equality when 4(x − 1)² = 9, i.e. x − 1 = 3/2, x = 5/2. Hence the minimum is 12 + 4 = 16. Check at x = 5/2: 4(2.5) + 9/(1.5) = 10 + 6 = 16. (Answering 12 forgets to add back the constant 4.) The answer is A.

promptHTML:
How many integer values of n satisfy

n2 < 3n + 40 ?
explanation: Rearrange: n² − 3n − 40 < 0, which factors as (n − 8)(n + 5) < 0. The product of the two factors is negative exactly when n lies strictly between the roots: −5 < n < 8. The integers in this range are −4, −3, …, 7, which is 7 − (−4) + 1 = 12 values. Note the endpoints fail: n = −5 gives 25 = 25 and n = 8 gives 64 = 64, and the inequality is strict. (Answering 13 or 14 comes from wrongly including one or both endpoints.) The answer is D.

promptHTML: Positive real numbers x and y satisfy 2x + 5y = 40. What is the maximum possible value of the product xy?
explanation: Apply AM–GM to the two terms 2x and 5y: (2x + 5y)/2 ≥ √(2x · 5y), so 20 ≥ √(10xy). Squaring: 400 ≥ 10xy, hence xy ≤ 40. Equality holds when 2x = 5y = 20, i.e. x = 10, y = 4, which indeed satisfies the constraint and gives xy = 40. (Answering 400 forgets to divide by the coefficient product 10; 20 comes from halving the correct answer.) The answer is B.

promptHTML:
How many integer values of x satisfy

|x − 3| > 2|x| ?
explanation: Both sides are non-negative, so squaring preserves the inequality: (x − 3)² > 4x², i.e. x² − 6x + 9 > 4x², so 3x² + 6x − 9 < 0. Dividing by 3: x² + 2x − 3 < 0, which factors as (x + 3)(x − 1) < 0, giving −3 < x < 1. The integers are −2, −1, 0: three values. Check x = 0: 3 > 0 true; x = −3: 6 > 6 false (correctly excluded); x = 1: 2 > 2 false. (Answering 4 or 5 comes from including an endpoint.) The answer is E.

promptHTML:
Over all real numbers x, what is the minimum value of

(x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3)(x + 4) ?
explanation: Pair the outer and inner factors: (x + 1)(x + 4) = x² + 5x + 4 and (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 5x + 6. Let u = x² + 5x + 5, so the product is (u − 1)(u + 1) = u² − 1 ≥ −1. The minimum −1 is attained when u = 0, i.e. x² + 5x + 5 = 0, which has real solutions x = (−5 ± √5)/2, so the bound is achieved. (Answering 0 assumes the product of four factors can't go negative; it can, when exactly one or three factors are negative.) The answer is B.

promptHTML: Let f(x) = 2x + 3, and let f<sup>(n)</sup> denote f composed with itself n times, so f<sup>(2)</sup>(x) = f(f(x)). What is the value of f<sup>(5)</sup>(1)?
explanation: Iterate directly: f(1) = 5; f(5) = 13; f(13) = 29; f(29) = 61; f(61) = 125. So f<sup>(5)</sup>(1) = 125. Alternatively, note f<sup>(n)</sup>(x) = 2<sup>n</sup>x + 3(2<sup>n</sup> − 1) (each iteration doubles and adds 3), so f<sup>(5)</sup>(1) = 32 · 1 + 3 · 31 = 32 + 93 = 125. (Answering 61 stops one iteration early; 93 is only the constant part 3(2⁵ − 1).) The answer is D.

promptHTML: A function f satisfies f(2x + 1) = 4x<sup>2</sup> + 6x + 5 for every real number x. What is the minimum value of f over all real inputs?
explanation: Find f explicitly. Let t = 2x + 1, so x = (t − 1)/2. Then f(t) = 4·[(t − 1)/2]² + 6·(t − 1)/2 + 5 = (t − 1)² + 3(t − 1) + 5 = t² + t + 3. As x runs over all reals, t = 2x + 1 also covers all reals, so we minimise t² + t + 3: the vertex is at t = −1/2, giving 1/4 − 1/2 + 3 = 11/4. (Answering 3 comes from minimising the original expression in x at x = 0 without completing the square: the true minimum of 4x² + 6x + 5 is at x = −3/4.) The answer is C.

promptHTML:
What is the value of x that satisfies

9x − 3x+1 = 54 ?
explanation: Write everything in terms of t = 3<sup>x</sup>. Since 9<sup>x</sup> = (3<sup>x</sup>)² = t² and 3<sup>x+1</sup> = 3t, the equation becomes t² − 3t − 54 = 0, which factors as (t − 9)(t + 6) = 0. Since t = 3<sup>x</sup> > 0, we must have t = 9 (the root t = −6 is rejected). Then 3<sup>x</sup> = 9 gives x = 2. Check: 9² − 3³ = 81 − 27 = 54. The answer is B.

promptHTML: A function f, defined for all real numbers, satisfies f(x) − f(x − 1) = 4x for every real x, and f(0) = 3. What is the value of f(10)?
explanation: Telescope from 0 up to 10: f(10) − f(0) = [f(10) − f(9)] + [f(9) − f(8)] + … + [f(1) − f(0)] = 4·10 + 4·9 + … + 4·1 = 4(1 + 2 + … + 10) = 4 · 55 = 220. Hence f(10) = 3 + 220 = 223. (Answering 220 forgets to add f(0) = 3; 203 comes from using 4·(1 + … + 10) = 200 via the wrong sum 50.) The answer is E.

promptHTML:
Let f(x) = 4x / (4x + 2). What is the value of

f(1/5) + f(2/5) + f(3/5) + f(4/5) ?
explanation: Key identity: f(x) + f(1 − x) = 1. Indeed f(1 − x) = 4<sup>1−x</sup>/(4<sup>1−x</sup> + 2) = 4/(4 + 2·4<sup>x</sup>) = 2/(4<sup>x</sup> + 2), so f(x) + f(1 − x) = (4<sup>x</sup> + 2)/(4<sup>x</sup> + 2) = 1. The four arguments pair up as (1/5, 4/5) and (2/5, 3/5), each pair summing to 1, so the total is 1 + 1 = 2. (Answering 4 treats every term as roughly 1; answering 1 pairs all four terms into a single unit.) The answer is A.

promptHTML: In an arithmetic progression, the 5th term is 31 and the 31st term is 5. What is the 36th term?
explanation: The common difference is d = (a<sub>31</sub> − a<sub>5</sub>)/(31 − 5) = (5 − 31)/26 = −1. Then a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>5</sub> + (n − 5)d = 31 − (n − 5) = 36 − n. So a<sub>36</sub> = 36 − 36 = 0. (This is the general fact: if the pth term is q and the qth term is p, the (p + q)th term is 0. Answering −1 overshoots by one step, a classic off-by-one.) The answer is C.

promptHTML: The three numbers x, x + 9, and x + 45 form a geometric progression (in that order). What is the common ratio of the progression?
explanation: In a GP the middle term squared equals the product of its neighbours: (x + 9)² = x(x + 45). Expanding: x² + 18x + 81 = x² + 45x, so 81 = 27x and x = 3. The terms are 3, 12, 48, and the common ratio is 12/3 = 4. Check: 48/12 = 4 as well. (Answering 12 confuses the second term with the ratio; answering 3 confuses x itself with the ratio.) The answer is D.

promptHTML:
Evaluate the sum

1/(√1 + √2) + 1/(√2 + √3) + 1/(√3 + √4) + … + 1/(√99 + √100).
explanation: Rationalise each term: 1/(√k + √(k+1)) = (√(k+1) − √k)/[(k+1) − k] = √(k+1) − √k. The sum telescopes: (√2 − √1) + (√3 − √2) + … + (√100 − √99) = √100 − √1 = 10 − 1 = 9. (Answering 10 forgets to subtract √1; 99 terms does not mean the answer relates to 99.) The answer is A.

promptHTML: Three positive numbers in geometric progression have sum 21, and the sum of their reciprocals is 7/12. What is the largest of the three numbers?
explanation: Write the terms as a/r, a, ar. Their sum is a(1/r + 1 + r) = 21. The reciprocals 1/(a/r), 1/a, 1/(ar) sum to (1/a)(r + 1 + 1/r) = 7/12 — the same bracket appears in both. Dividing the equations: a² = 21 ÷ (7/12) = 36, so a = 6 (terms are positive). Then 6(1/r + 1 + r) = 21 gives r + 1/r = 5/2, so r = 2 or r = 1/2. Either way the terms are 3, 6, 12, and the largest is 12. Check: 3 + 6 + 12 = 21; 1/3 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 7/12. (Answering 6 gives the middle term, not the largest.) The answer is E.

promptHTML: A worker saves $200 in the first month and in each subsequent month saves $40 more than in the previous month. After how many months will her total savings first reach exactly $5040?
explanation: The monthly savings form an AP with first term 200 and common difference 40. The total after n months is S<sub>n</sub> = (n/2)[2·200 + (n − 1)·40] = n(200 + 20(n − 1)) = 20n² + 180n. Set 20n² + 180n = 5040 and divide by 20: n² + 9n − 252 = 0, which factors as (n − 12)(n + 21) = 0. Since n > 0, n = 12. Check: S<sub>12</sub> = 20·144 + 180·12 = 2880 + 2160 = 5040. The answer is B.

promptHTML: In triangle PQR, PQ = 7, PR = 8, and the angle at P measures 120°. What is the length of side QR?
explanation: Use the Law of Cosines on the angle at P: QR² = PQ² + PR² − 2·PQ·PR·cos(120°). Since cos(120°) = −1/2, the subtraction becomes an addition: QR² = 49 + 64 − 2(7)(8)(−1/2) = 113 + 56 = 169, so QR = 13. The trap answer √57 comes from wrongly using cos(120°) = +1/2 and computing 113 − 56 = 57. The answer is D.

promptHTML: The three medians of a triangle have lengths 9, 12, and 15. What is the area of the triangle?
explanation: Key fact: the area of a triangle equals 4/3 times the area of the triangle formed by its three medians. Here the medians 9, 12, 15 themselves form a right triangle, because 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15². The median triangle's area is (1/2)(9)(12) = 54. So the original triangle's area is (4/3)(54) = 72. Choosing 54 means you stopped at the median triangle; choosing 40.5 means you multiplied by 3/4 instead of 4/3. The answer is C.

promptHTML: A point lies inside an equilateral triangle. The perpendicular distances from this point to the three sides of the triangle are 3, 4, and 5. What is the area of the triangle?
explanation: Viviani's theorem: for any interior point of an equilateral triangle, the sum of the perpendicular distances to the three sides equals the altitude of the triangle. So the altitude h = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. For side length s, h = (s√3)/2, so s = 24/√3 = 8√3. Area = (√3/4)s² = (√3/4)(192) = 48√3. (Check: connecting the point to the vertices splits the triangle into three pieces of total area (1/2)s(3 + 4 + 5) = (1/2)(8√3)(12) = 48√3.) Using 12 as the side length instead of the altitude gives the trap 36√3. The answer is B.

promptHTML: A right triangle has an inscribed circle of radius 6 and a circumscribed circle of radius 14.5. What is the area of the triangle?
explanation: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumscribed circle, so c = 2(14.5) = 29. For a right triangle with legs a, b: inradius r = (a + b − c)/2, so 6 = (a + b − 29)/2, giving a + b = 41. The semiperimeter is s = (41 + 29)/2 = 35, and area = r·s = 6 × 35 = 210. (Indeed the triangle is 20-21-29: 20 + 21 − 29 = 12 = 2r, and (1/2)(20)(21) = 210.) Choosing 420 means you forgot the 1/2 in the leg product; 105 is halving 210 a second time. The answer is E.

promptHTML: An isosceles triangle has perimeter 32, and the altitude drawn to its base (the unequal side) has length 8. What is the area of the triangle?
explanation: Let the base be 2x and each equal side be a, so 2a + 2x = 32, i.e. a = 16 − x. The altitude to the base bisects it, so a² = 8² + x²: (16 − x)² = 64 + x², which gives 256 − 32x = 64, so x = 6. The base is 12 and the legs are 10 (check: 10 + 10 + 12 = 32). Area = (1/2)(12)(8) = 48. Choosing 96 means you forgot the 1/2; 60 comes from wrongly using a leg (10) with the altitude. The answer is A.

promptHTML: In a triangle, two of the sides have lengths 7 and 9, and the median drawn to the third side has length 7. What is the length of the third side?
explanation: Apollonius' theorem: if m is the median to side a, and b, c are the other two sides, then b² + c² = 2m² + a²/2. Substituting: 7² + 9² = 2(7²) + a²/2, so 130 = 98 + a²/2, giving a²/2 = 32, a² = 64, a = 8. Dropping the factor 2 on the median term gives a² = 162 (the trap 9√2); writing 2a² instead of a²/2 gives a = 4. The answer is C.

promptHTML: A chord of length 16 is drawn in a circle of radius 10. M is the midpoint of the chord. What is the distance from M to the nearest point on the circle?
explanation: The perpendicular from the center O to the chord meets it at its midpoint M. Half the chord is 8, so OM = √(10² − 8²) = √36 = 6. The nearest point of the circle to M lies along ray OM extended past M to the circle: its distance from M is (radius) − OM = 10 − 6 = 4. Answering 6 means you stopped at the center-to-chord distance instead of continuing to the circle. The answer is A.

promptHTML: Two circles with radii 5 and 3 lie completely outside each other, and the distance between their centers is 17. A common internal tangent is drawn (a line tangent to both circles that crosses the segment joining the centers). What is the length of this tangent segment between its two points of tangency?
explanation: For a common internal tangent, the tangent length is √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²), because shifting one radius across creates a right triangle whose legs are the tangent length and r₁ + r₂ = 8, with hypotenuse d = 17. Length = √(17² − 8²) = √(289 − 64) = √225 = 15. Using the difference of radii (r₁ − r₂ = 2) is the external-tangent formula and gives the trap √285. The answer is B.

promptHTML: A chord of a circle of radius 12 subtends an angle of 120° at the center. What is the area of the minor segment, the region enclosed between the chord and the minor arc?
explanation: Segment area = sector area − triangle area. Sector: (120/360)π(12²) = (1/3)(144π) = 48π. Triangle formed by the two radii and the chord: (1/2)r²sin(120°) = (1/2)(144)(√3/2) = 36√3. So the minor segment has area 48π − 36√3. Forgetting the 1/2 in the triangle formula gives 48π − 72√3; adding instead of subtracting gives 48π + 36√3. The answer is D.

promptHTML: From an external point P, two tangent segments are drawn to a circle, each of length 12, and the angle between the two tangents at P is 60°. What is the radius of the circle?
explanation: Let O be the center and T a point of tangency. OT is perpendicular to the tangent PT, and the line PO bisects the 60° angle, so angle OPT = 30°. In right triangle OTP: tan(30°) = OT/PT, so r = 12·tan(30°) = 12/√3 = 4√3. Using tan(60°) instead of the half-angle gives the trap 12√3; answering 6 comes from wrongly treating r as 12·sin(30°) with 12 as a hypotenuse. The answer is C.

promptHTML: Three circles are mutually tangent externally (each pair touches at exactly one point, with the circles outside one another). The distances between the three pairs of centers are 6, 8, and 10. What is the radius of the smallest circle?
explanation: When two circles are externally tangent, the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii. Call the radii a, b, c with a + b = 6, a + c = 8, b + c = 10. Adding all three: 2(a + b + c) = 24, so a + b + c = 12. Then c = 12 − 6 = 6, b = 12 − 8 = 4, a = 12 − 10 = 2. The smallest radius is 2. Answering 3 comes from just halving the smallest center distance, which would only be right if that pair had equal radii. The answer is E.

promptHTML: A quadrilateral has vertices, taken in order, at (1, 1), (7, 2), (8, 6), and (2, 5). What is its area?
explanation: Use the shoelace formula on the vertices in order. Down-products: (1)(2) + (7)(6) + (8)(5) + (2)(1) = 2 + 42 + 40 + 2 = 86. Up-products: (1)(7) + (2)(8) + (6)(2) + (5)(1) = 7 + 16 + 12 + 5 = 40. Area = |86 − 40|/2 = 46/2 = 23. Forgetting to halve at the end gives the trap 46. The answer is A.

promptHTML: A line with negative slope passes through the point (2, 3) and, together with the positive x-axis and positive y-axis, encloses a triangle. What is the least possible area of this triangle?
explanation: Write the line in intercept form x/a + y/b = 1 with a, b > 0. Passing through (2, 3) means 2/a + 3/b = 1. By AM-GM, 1 = 2/a + 3/b ≥ 2√(6/(ab)), so √(6/(ab)) ≤ 1/2, giving ab ≥ 24. The triangle's area is ab/2 ≥ 12, with equality when 2/a = 3/b = 1/2, i.e. a = 4, b = 6 (check: 2/4 + 3/6 = 1). Minimum area = 12. Answering 6 is the common error of taking the product of the coordinates (2)(3) as the area. The answer is D.

promptHTML: The point P(3, 4) is rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin to give the point P′. What is the distance between P and P′?
explanation: A 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin sends (x, y) to (−y, x), so P′ = (−4, 3). Distance PP′ = √((3 − (−4))² + (4 − 3)²) = √(49 + 1) = √50 = 5√2. Shortcut: P and P′ both lie on a circle of radius 5 about the origin, separated by a 90° central angle, so PP′ is the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle with legs 5, i.e. 5√2. Answering 5 confuses the distance from the origin with the distance moved; 10 would be a 180° rotation. The answer is B.

promptHTML: A right triangle has its two legs along the positive x-axis and positive y-axis, with the right angle at the origin. The centroid of the triangle is the point (8, 6). What is the length of the hypotenuse?
explanation: Let the vertices be O(0, 0), A(a, 0), and B(0, b). The centroid is the average of the vertices: ((a + 0 + 0)/3, (0 + b + 0)/3) = (a/3, b/3). So a/3 = 8 and b/3 = 6, giving a = 24 and b = 18. Hypotenuse AB = √(24² + 18²) = √(576 + 324) = √900 = 30. Answering 10 = √(8² + 6²) means you forgot to scale the centroid coordinates up by 3. The answer is E.

promptHTML: A rectangular sheet of paper measures 44 cm by 20 cm. It is rolled up along its longer side to form a hollow cylinder (so the 44 cm edge becomes the circumference of the base, and the height is 20 cm). Taking π = 22/7, what is the volume enclosed by the cylinder, in cubic centimeters?
explanation: The circumference of the base is 44, so 2πr = 44 gives r = 44 × 7/(2 × 22) = 7 cm, and the height is h = 20 cm. Volume = πr²h = (22/7)(49)(20) = 22 × 7 × 20 = 3080 cm³. Rolling along the shorter side instead (20 as circumference) gives the trap 1400; treating 44 as the radius-related diameter leads to other wrong values. The answer is D.

promptHTML: A metal pipe is a hollow cylinder of length 21 cm. Its outer radius is 5 cm and its inner radius is 3 cm. Taking π = 22/7, what is the volume of the metal in the pipe, in cubic centimeters?
explanation: The metal is the region between the two cylinders: V = π(R² − r²)h = (22/7)(5² − 3²)(21) = (22/7)(16)(21) = 22 × 16 × 3 = 1056 cm³. The classic mistake is computing π(R − r)²h = (22/7)(4)(21) = 264: you must subtract the squares, not square the difference. Choosing 1650 means you took the full outer cylinder and forgot to remove the hollow; 594 is the inner (hollow) volume itself. The answer is A.

promptHTML: A sector of a circle has radius 15 cm and central angle 216°. The two straight edges of the sector are brought together and joined so that it forms a right circular cone (the sector's arc becomes the cone's base circle). What is the volume of the cone, in cubic centimeters?
explanation: The sector's radius becomes the cone's slant height: l = 15. The arc length becomes the base circumference: arc = (216/360)(2π)(15) = (3/5)(30π) = 18π, so 2πr = 18π and r = 9. The vertical height is h = √(l² − r²) = √(225 − 81) = 12. Volume = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(81)(12) = 324π cm³. Using the slant height 15 in place of the vertical height gives the trap 405π; forgetting the 1/3 gives 972π. The answer is E.

promptHTML: A right triangle has legs of length 8 cm and 15 cm. It is rotated one full turn about its 15 cm leg, sweeping out a solid of revolution. What is the volume of this solid, in cubic centimeters?
explanation: Rotating a right triangle about one leg produces a cone whose height is that leg and whose base radius is the other leg. Here h = 15 and r = 8, so V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(64)(15) = 320π cm³. Rotating about the 8 cm leg instead would give (1/3)π(225)(8) = 600π, the main trap; forgetting the 1/3 gives 960π. The answer is B.

promptHTML: The surface area of a solid sphere increases by 44%. By what percentage does the volume of the sphere increase?
explanation: Surface area scales as r², so the new-to-old area ratio is 1.44, which means the radius scales by √1.44 = 1.2 (a 20% increase). Volume scales as r³, so the volume ratio is 1.2³ = 1.728, i.e. a 72.8% increase. Answering 172.8% confuses the ratio (the new volume is 172.8% OF the old) with the increase; 44% wrongly carries the area change straight over to volume; 20% stops at the radius. The answer is C.

promptHTML: When 2026<sup>2026</sup> is written out in full, what are its final two digits?
explanation: Only the last two digits of the base matter: 2026 ≡ 26 (mod 100). Powers of 26: 26² = 676 ≡ 76, and 76 is idempotent (76 × 76 = 5776 ≡ 76), while 76 × 26 = 1976 ≡ 76. So 26n ≡ 76 for every n ≥ 2. Numbers ending in 76 absorb everything — recognising the idempotent pair 25/76 kills this instantly.

promptHTML: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 satisfy n² ≡ n (mod 100)?
explanation: n(n − 1) must be divisible by 4 and by 25. Since n and n − 1 are coprime, each prime power must divide one of them: n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4) AND n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 25). CRT gives 2 × 2 = 4 residues mod 100: n ≡ 0, 1, 25, 76. In 1…100 these are 1, 25, 76, 100 — 4 integers (the “automorphic” endings).

promptHTML: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 500 leave a remainder of 3 when divided by 7 AND a remainder of 4 when divided by 9?
explanation: We need n ≡ 3 (mod 7) and n ≡ 4 (mod 9). Write n = 7k + 3 and require 7k + 3 ≡ 4 (mod 9), i.e. 7k ≡ 1 (mod 9). Since 7 × 4 = 28 ≡ 1 (mod 9), the inverse of 7 is 4, so k ≡ 4 (mod 9). Then n = 7(9m + 4) + 3 = 63m + 31. The solutions in range are 31, 94, 157, 220, 283, 346, 409, 472 — we need 63m + 31 ≤ 500, i.e. m ≤ 7.44, so m = 0, 1, …, 7. That is 8 values. Answering 7 is the classic off-by-one (forgetting m = 0). The answer is C.

promptHTML: Let N = 2<sup>2026</sup>. What is the remainder when N is divided by 100?
explanation: gcd(2, 100) ≠ 1, so Euler cannot be applied directly — split by CRT. Mod 4: 22026 ≡ 0. Mod 25: φ(25) = 20 and 2026 ≡ 6 (mod 20), so 22026 ≡ 26 = 64 ≡ 14 (mod 25). Seek x ≡ 0 (mod 4), x ≡ 14 (mod 25): x = 64. Applying φ(100) = 40 blindly to a non-coprime base is the trap.

promptHTML: Let N be the integer formed by writing the digit 1 exactly 32 times in a row (N = 111…1 with 32 ones). What is the remainder when N is divided by 37?
explanation: Key fact: 111 = 3 × 37, so any block of three consecutive 1s is divisible by 37 — and more generally the 30-digit repunit (ten blocks of 111 spaced by powers of 1000) is divisible by 37. Write N = R<sub>30</sub> × 10<sup>2</sup> + 11, where R<sub>30</sub> is the repunit with 30 ones. Since 37 divides R<sub>30</sub>, we get N ≡ 11 (mod 37). Verification of the block argument: R<sub>30</sub> = 111 × (10<sup>27</sup> + 10<sup>24</sup> + … + 1). Answering 0 assumes 37 divides all repunits; answering 1 comes from miscounting 32 as 31 = 30 + 1. The answer is B.

promptHTML: How many positive divisors of 10! (the product of all integers from 1 to 10) are odd?
explanation: Prime-factorise 10!: exponent of 2 is ⌊10/2⌋ + ⌊10/4⌋ + ⌊10/8⌋ = 5 + 2 + 1 = 8; exponent of 3 is 3 + 1 = 4; exponent of 5 is 2; exponent of 7 is 1. So 10! = 2<sup>8</sup> × 3<sup>4</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7. An odd divisor uses no factor of 2, so count divisors of the odd part 3<sup>4</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7: (4+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 30. Answering 270 counts ALL divisors (9 × 5 × 3 × 2); 240 counts the even ones. The answer is C.

promptHTML: How many positive divisors of 8400 are multiples of 12?
explanation: Factorise: 8400 = 84 × 100 = (2<sup>2</sup> × 3 × 7) × (2<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>) = 2<sup>4</sup> × 3 × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7. A divisor 2<sup>a</sup>3<sup>b</sup>5<sup>c</sup>7<sup>d</sup> is a multiple of 12 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 exactly when a ≥ 2 and b ≥ 1. Count the choices: a ∈ {2, 3, 4} gives 3 options; b must be 1 (only 1 option since the exponent of 3 in 8400 is 1); c ∈ {0, 1, 2} gives 3; d ∈ {0, 1} gives 2. Total: 3 × 1 × 3 × 2 = 18. Equivalently, these are the divisors of 8400/12 = 700 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7, which has 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 divisors. Answering 60 counts all divisors of 8400. The answer is E.

promptHTML: Let N = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5 × 7 × 11. In how many ways can N be written as a product a × b of two positive integers with gcd(a, b) = 1, where the order of the factors does not matter?
explanation: If gcd(a, b) = 1 and ab = N, then for each prime, its ENTIRE prime power must go wholly to a or wholly to b (splitting a prime between them would make it a common factor). N has exactly 5 distinct primes (2, 3, 5, 7, 11), so there are 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 ordered assignments, giving 32 ordered pairs (a, b). Since N is not a perfect square, no pair has a = b, so the number of unordered pairs is 32 ÷ 2 = 16. (Note the pair 1 × N is legitimately coprime and IS counted.) Answering 32 forgets to halve; 15 wrongly excludes the pair (1, N); 8 miscounts the distinct primes as 4. The answer is B.

promptHTML: Let P = 5 × 10 × 15 × … × 100 (the product of all multiples of 5 from 5 to 100). How many consecutive zeros are there at the right-hand end of P?
explanation: Factor out 5 from each of the 20 terms: P = 5<sup>20</sup> × (1 × 2 × … × 20) = 5<sup>20</sup> × 20!. Trailing zeros = min(exponent of 2, exponent of 5). Exponent of 5: 20 (factored out) + exponent of 5 in 20! = 20 + (⌊20/5⌋ + ⌊20/25⌋) = 20 + 4 = 24. Exponent of 2: only from 20!, namely ⌊20/2⌋ + ⌊20/4⌋ + ⌊20/8⌋ + ⌊20/16⌋ = 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 18. Here the 2s are scarcer than the 5s (the reverse of the usual factorial situation!), so the number of trailing zeros is min(18, 24) = 18. Answering 24 counts only the fives — the classic trap. The answer is D.

promptHTML: What is the smallest positive integer that has exactly 28 positive divisors?
explanation: If n = p<sup>a</sup>q<sup>b</sup>…, the divisor count is (a+1)(b+1)… = 28. Factorisations of 28: 28; 14 × 2; 7 × 4; 7 × 2 × 2. These give exponent patterns (27), (13, 1), (6, 3), (6, 1, 1). Assign the largest exponents to the smallest primes and compare: 2<sup>27</sup> (huge); 2<sup>13</sup> × 3 = 24576; 2<sup>6</sup> × 3<sup>3</sup> = 64 × 27 = 1728; 2<sup>6</sup> × 3 × 5 = 64 × 15 = 960. The smallest is 960. Check: 960 = 2<sup>6</sup> × 3 × 5 has (6+1)(1+1)(1+1) = 28 divisors. Note 720 has 30 divisors and 840 has 32 — small numbers with MANY divisors, but not exactly 28. The answer is A.

promptHTML: The difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on a certain sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹620. What is the sum?
explanation: For 3 years at rate r, CI − SI = P[(1 + r)<sup>3</sup> − 1 − 3r] = P(3r<sup>2</sup> + r<sup>3</sup>). With r = 0.1: 3(0.01) + 0.001 = 0.031. So 0.031P = 620, giving P = 620 ÷ 0.031 = 20,000. Verify: CI on 20,000 at 10% for 3 years = 20,000(1.331 − 1) = 6,620; SI = 20,000 × 0.10 × 3 = 6,000; difference = 620. Answering ₹62,000 comes from using the 2-year formula Pr<sup>2</sup> = 620 by mistake. The answer is B.

promptHTML: A contractor plans to build a wall in 30 days using 24 men working 8 hours a day. After 12 days (work having proceeded exactly on schedule), 8 men leave the site. How many hours per day must the remaining men work so that the wall is still finished on day 30?
explanation: Total work = 24 men × 30 days × 8 h/day = 5,760 man-hours. Work done in the first 12 days = 24 × 12 × 8 = 2,304 man-hours, leaving 5,760 − 2,304 = 3,456 man-hours. The remaining 16 men have 30 − 12 = 18 days, so the required hours per day = 3,456 ÷ (16 × 18) = 3,456 ÷ 288 = 12. Sanity check: the workforce dropped by a factor 16/24 = 2/3, so daily hours must rise by 3/2: 8 × 3/2 = 12. The answer is D.

promptHTML: A train passes a signal pole in 12 seconds and a 360-metre-long platform in 30 seconds, travelling at a constant speed. How long will the same train take to completely cross a 240-metre-long train travelling in the opposite direction at 36 km/h?
explanation: Let the train's length be L and speed v. Passing the pole: L = 12v. Passing the platform: L + 360 = 30v. Subtracting: 360 = 18v, so v = 20 m/s and L = 240 m. The oncoming train: 36 km/h = 10 m/s, length 240 m. For opposite directions the relative speed is 20 + 10 = 30 m/s, and the distance to cover is the sum of the lengths, 240 + 240 = 480 m. Time = 480 ÷ 30 = 16 seconds. Answering 48 comes from subtracting the speeds (same-direction formula); 24 comes from forgetting to add the other train's speed (480 ÷ 20); 12 uses only one train's length. The answer is A.

promptHTML: A tank contains 60 litres of a solution that is 30% acid. How many litres of the solution must be drawn off and replaced with pure acid so that the tank contains a 44% acid solution?
explanation: Suppose x litres of solution are removed and replaced with pure acid. The removed solution carries away 0.3x litres of acid, and x litres of pure acid come in. Final acid = 0.3(60 − x) + x = 18 + 0.7x litres. Setting this equal to 44% of 60 litres = 26.4: 18 + 0.7x = 26.4, so 0.7x = 8.4 and x = 12. Verify: remove 12 L (leaving 14.4 L acid in 48 L), add 12 L pure acid: 26.4/60 = 44%. Answering 8.4 treats the needed 14-percentage-point rise as litres directly; 14 comes from dropping the 0.7 factor incorrectly. The answer is C.

promptHTML: Walking from home to school at 4 km/h, a student arrives 6 minutes late. Walking the same route at 6 km/h, she arrives 10 minutes early. What is the distance from her home to school?
explanation: Let the distance be d km. The time difference between the slow trip and the fast trip is 6 + 10 = 16 minutes = 16/60 hours (late by 6 versus early by 10 spans the FULL 16-minute gap). So d/4 − d/6 = 16/60. The left side is d(3 − 2)/12 = d/12, hence d/12 = 4/15, giving d = 48/15 = 3.2 km. Verify: at 4 km/h the trip takes 48 min; at 6 km/h it takes 32 min; difference = 16 min, consistent with 6 late/10 early around a 42-minute deadline. The classic error is using only 6 (or only 10) minutes as the gap instead of their sum. The answer is E.

promptHTML: The monthly incomes of Aditi and Bala are in the ratio 5 : 4, and their monthly expenditures are in the ratio 3 : 2. If each of them saves ₹6,000 per month, what is Aditi's monthly income?
explanation: Let the incomes be 5x and 4x, and the expenditures be 3y and 2y. Savings = income − expenditure, so 5x − 3y = 6,000 and 4x − 2y = 6,000. From the second equation: 2x − y = 3,000, so y = 2x − 3,000. Substitute into the first: 5x − 3(2x − 3,000) = 6,000, i.e. 5x − 6x + 9,000 = 6,000, so x = 3,000 (and y = 3,000). Aditi's income = 5x = ₹15,000. Verify: Aditi 15,000 − 9,000 = 6,000 saved; Bala 12,000 − 6,000 = 6,000 saved. Answering ₹12,000 gives Bala's income instead of Aditi's. The answer is C.

promptHTML: A round table has 12 chairs equally spaced around it. In how many ways can 4 of the 12 chairs be selected so that no two selected chairs are adjacent to each other?
explanation: For choosing k non-adjacent positions from n in a CIRCLE, the count is [n/(n−k)] × C(n−k, k). Here n = 12, k = 4: (12/8) × C(8,4) = 1.5 × 70 = 105. Sanity check via cases: fix chair 1 as chosen or not. If chair 1 is chosen, chairs 2 and 12 are forbidden, and we need 3 non-adjacent chairs from the 9 chairs 3–11 in a LINE: C(9−3+1, 3) = C(7,3) = 35. If chair 1 is not chosen, we need 4 non-adjacent chairs from chairs 2–12 in a line: C(11−4+1, 4) = C(8,4) = 70. Total = 35 + 70 = 105. Trap answers: C(9,4) = 126 uses the straight-line formula and ignores that the first and last chairs are neighbors in a circle; C(8,4) = 70 drops the circular correction factor; C(12,4) = 495 ignores the adjacency restriction entirely. The answer is C.

promptHTML: Using the letters of the word PEPPER (which contains three P's, two E's, and one R), how many distinct 4-letter arrangements can be formed? Each letter may be used no more times than it appears in PEPPER.
explanation: Split by how many of each letter the 4-letter word uses, writing (p, e, r) for the counts of P, E, R with p ≤ 3, e ≤ 2, r ≤ 1 and p + e + r = 4. The possibilities and their arrangement counts: (3,1,0): 4!/3! = 4; (3,0,1): 4!/3! = 4; (2,2,0): 4!/(2!·2!) = 6; (2,1,1): 4!/2! = 12; (1,2,1): 4!/2! = 12. Total = 4 + 4 + 6 + 12 + 12 = 38. Note (0,2,1) and similar fail because e + r can contribute at most 3 letters, so at least one P is forced except when p ≥ 1 anyway. Trap answers: 360 = 6P4 treats all six letters as distinct; 180 divides 360 by 2! correcting only for the E's; 60 = 6!/(3!2!) counts arrangements of the FULL 6-letter word, not 4-letter ones. The answer is A.

promptHTML: A club of 9 members must elect a president, a treasurer, and a secretary (three different people, one per office). Two particular members, Arjun and Bela, refuse to serve as officers at the same time (either may serve alone). How many valid ways are there to fill the three offices?
explanation: Count all assignments, then subtract the forbidden ones. Total with no restriction: 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 ordered choices. Forbidden = both Arjun and Bela hold offices: choose which 2 of the 3 offices they occupy and in what order (3 × 2 = 6 ways), then fill the remaining office from the other 7 members (7 ways): 6 × 7 = 42. Valid = 504 − 42 = 462. Trap answers: 504 ignores the restriction; 498 = 504 − 6 forgets to multiply by the 7 choices for the third officer; 420 = 504 − 84 double-counts the forbidden cases; 336 = 8 × 7 × 6 wrongly bans Bela from serving at all. The answer is D.

promptHTML: How many ordered triples of positive integers (x, y, z) satisfy x + y + z = 20 with the strict inequalities x < y < z?
explanation: First count ALL positive solutions of x + y + z = 20: C(19,2) = 171. Next remove solutions with a repeated value. Solutions with x = y: 2x + z = 20 forces x = 1, ..., 9 (z must stay positive), giving 9 solutions; by symmetry y = z and x = z also give 9 each; x = y = z would need 3x = 20, impossible. No solution is counted twice among these (that would require all three equal), so ordered solutions with all values DISTINCT = 171 − 27 = 144. Each set of three distinct values appears in 3! = 6 orders, but exactly one of those orders has x < y < z, so the count is 144/6 = 24. Trap answers: 171 forgets both the distinctness and ordering conditions; 144 counts all distinct-value orderings without imposing x < y < z; 27 is the number of repeated-value solutions; 18 comes from subtracting the 27 before dividing incorrectly. The answer is B.

promptHTML: How many 5-character strings can be formed using the letters A, B, and C (repetition allowed) if each of the three letters must appear at least once in the string?
explanation: Use inclusion–exclusion on the letters that are missing. Total strings: 3<sup>5</sup> = 243. Subtract strings missing at least one specific letter: 3 choices of missing letter, each leaving 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 strings, total 96. But strings using only ONE letter were subtracted twice, so add them back: 3 strings (AAAAA, BBBBB, CCCCC). Count = 243 − 96 + 3 = 150. Trap answers: 243 ignores the requirement; 147 = 243 − 96 forgets the add-back term; 96 is the subtracted quantity itself; 90 comes from a wrong surjection shortcut. The answer is E.

promptHTML: A fair six-sided die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability that at least two of the four rolls show the same number?
explanation: Use the complement: P(at least one repeat) = 1 − P(all four rolls distinct). All distinct: the first roll can be anything, then 5/6, 4/6, 3/6 for the next three, so P = (6 × 5 × 4 × 3)/6<sup>4</sup> = 360/1296 = 5/18. Therefore P(at least two match) = 1 − 5/18 = 13/18. Trap answers: 5/18 stops at the complement and forgets to subtract from 1; 671/1296 = 1 − (5/6)<sup>4</sup> wrongly demands only that rolls 2–4 differ from the first roll; 91/216 = 1 − (5/6)(4/6)(3/6)·… is the 3-roll version of the problem. The answer is A.

promptHTML: Two distinct integers are chosen at random from the integers 1 through 20 inclusive. What is the probability that their sum is divisible by 3?
explanation: Classify 1–20 by remainder mod 3: remainder 0: {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18} — 6 numbers; remainder 1: {1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19} — 7 numbers; remainder 2: {2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20} — 7 numbers. A sum is divisible by 3 when both numbers have remainder 0, or one has remainder 1 and the other remainder 2. Favorable pairs: C(6,2) + 7 × 7 = 15 + 49 = 64. Total pairs: C(20,2) = 190. Probability = 64/190 = 32/95. Trap answers: 49/190 forgets the both-remainder-0 pairs; 3/10 = 57/190 wrongly pairs remainder-1 with remainder-1 and remainder-2 with remainder-2 instead; 1/3 assumes divisibility by 3 is uniform, which fails because the remainder classes are unequal in size. The answer is C.

promptHTML: A fair coin is flipped 6 times in a row. What is the probability that heads never comes up on two consecutive flips?
explanation: Count length-n sequences of H/T with no HH. Let a<sub>n</sub> be that count. A valid sequence ends in T (append T to any valid sequence of length n−1) or ends in TH (append TH to any valid sequence of length n−2), so a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>n−1</sub> + a<sub>n−2</sub> with a<sub>1</sub> = 2, a<sub>2</sub> = 3. Then a<sub>3</sub> = 5, a<sub>4</sub> = 8, a<sub>5</sub> = 13, a<sub>6</sub> = 21. Probability = 21/2<sup>6</sup> = 21/64. Trap answers: 13/64 uses a<sub>5</sub> (off-by-one in the Fibonacci ladder); 17/32 = 34/64 overshoots to a<sub>7</sub>; 5/16 = 20/64 and 33/64 are near-miss miscounts from trying to subtract HH-containing strings position by position, which double-counts overlaps. The answer is E.

promptHTML: Ria and Sam play a table-tennis match that ends as soon as one of them has won 2 games (no game can be tied). Ria wins each game independently with probability 2/3. What is the probability that Ria wins the match?
explanation: Ria wins the match either 2–0 or 2–1. Win 2–0: she wins games 1 and 2: (2/3)<sup>2</sup> = 4/9. Win 2–1: games 1–2 split 1–1 (two orders: WL or LW), then she wins game 3: 2 × (2/3)(1/3)(2/3) = 8/27. Total = 4/9 + 8/27 = 12/27 + 8/27 = 20/27. Note this exceeds her single-game probability 2/3 = 18/27, as it should — a longer series favors the stronger player. Trap answers: 4/9 counts only the straight 2–0 win; 2/3 assumes the match probability equals the single-game probability; 16/27 forgets one of the two orders in the 2–1 path; 22/27 adds (2/3)(1/3)(2/3) twice plus 4/9 with an arithmetic slip. The answer is B.

promptHTML: A hat contains 8 slips of paper numbered 1 through 8. Three slips are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that the median (middle value) of the three numbers drawn is exactly 5?
explanation: For the median to be 5, one drawn number must be 5 itself, one must be smaller, and one must be larger. Numbers smaller than 5: {1, 2, 3, 4} — 4 choices. Numbers larger than 5: {6, 7, 8} — 3 choices. Favorable selections: 1 × 4 × 3 = 12. Total selections: C(8,3) = 56. Probability = 12/56 = 3/14. Trap answers: 1/8 assumes each of the 8 values is equally likely to be the median (they are not — extreme values can rarely be the middle); 15/56 uses 5 numbers below instead of 4; 9/28 = 18/56 miscounts by including 5 among the smaller values; 5/28 = 10/56 drops two of the favorable pairs. The answer is D.

promptHTML: At a conference, each of the 180 attendees drank at least one of coffee, tea, or juice during the breakfast break. Exactly 100 drank coffee, 90 drank tea, and 75 drank juice. Exactly 55 attendees drank exactly two of the three beverages. How many attendees drank all three beverages?
explanation: Let e<sub>1</sub>, e<sub>2</sub>, e<sub>3</sub> be the numbers who drank exactly one, exactly two, and exactly three beverages. Two facts: (1) everyone drank something, so e<sub>1</sub> + e<sub>2</sub> + e<sub>3</sub> = 180; (2) summing the individual beverage counts counts each exactly-two person twice and each exactly-three person three times, so e<sub>1</sub> + 2e<sub>2</sub> + 3e<sub>3</sub> = 100 + 90 + 75 = 265. Subtracting (1) from (2): e<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sub>3</sub> = 85. With e<sub>2</sub> = 55: 2e<sub>3</sub> = 30, so e<sub>3</sub> = 15. Trap answers: 30 is 2e<sub>3</sub>, forgetting the final division by 2; 25 and 10 come from treating the 55 as the sum of pairwise intersections |A∩B| + |B∩C| + |A∩C| (which actually equals 55 + 3 × 15 = 100); 45 is 3e<sub>3</sub>. The answer is A.

promptHTML: A market-research firm surveyed 150 shoppers about two snack brands. Exactly 90 shoppers like brand A and exactly 75 like brand B (these counts include anyone who likes both). Exactly 95 shoppers like exactly one of the two brands. How many of the 150 shoppers like neither brand?
explanation: Let b = number who like both brands. Then those who like ONLY A number 90 − b, and only B number 75 − b, so exactly-one = (90 − b) + (75 − b) = 165 − 2b. Setting 165 − 2b = 95 gives b = 35. People who like at least one brand = exactly-one + both = 95 + 35 = 130. Neither = 150 − 130 = 20. Trap answers: 35 is the both-brands count, not what was asked; 55 = 150 − 95 forgets to remove the both group from the remainder; 15 = 90 + 75 − 150 wrongly assumes every shopper likes at least one brand; 30 halves the exactly-one deficit incorrectly. The answer is C.

promptHTML:
In a survey of 100 freelancers about three tools — P, Q, and R — the results were:
• 48 use P, 45 use Q, 42 use R.
• 18 use both P and Q, 17 use both Q and R, 16 use both P and R (each of these counts includes those who use all three).
• 7 use all three tools.

How many of the 100 freelancers use exactly one of the three tools?
explanation: Work region by region. Users of exactly two tools: P&Q only = 18 − 7 = 11; Q&R only = 17 − 7 = 10; P&R only = 16 − 7 = 9; total exactly-two = 30. Only P = 48 − 11 − 9 − 7 = 21; only Q = 45 − 11 − 10 − 7 = 17; only R = 42 − 10 − 9 − 7 = 16. Exactly one = 21 + 17 + 16 = 54. (Check: union = 54 + 30 + 7 = 91, matching 48 + 45 + 42 − 18 − 17 − 16 + 7 = 91, so 9 freelancers use none — consistent.) Trap answers: 91 is the union (at least one tool); 61 = 91 − 30 forgets to also remove the all-three group; 33 = 135 − 2(51) applies the exactly-one formula but drops the +3 × 7 correction term; 44 miscounts one of the pairwise-only regions.
